en: MSuAv [1] Furthermore, Great King, listen to that benefit for sentient beings which was performed by me while seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
MSuAv [2] Long ago, Great King, there was a king named Mahāsudarśana, who was endowed with the seven jewels and the four superhuman powers (*ṛddhi*). Which were they?
With the seven jewels, namely:

the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel as the seventh. With which four human supernormal powers is the king endowed?
Great King Mahāsudarśana was long-lived and remained for a long time. He spent eighty-four thousand years in princely play,
eighty-four thousand years exercising the office of crown prince,
and eighty-four thousand years exercising the office of great king.

For eighty-four thousand years, he practiced the celibate life of a royal seer (*rājarṣi*). Great King, that King Mahāsudarśana was long-lived and remained for a long time, practicing the celibate life of a royal seer for eighty-four thousand years;
this is called the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of King Mahāsudarśana.

Furthermore, Great King, King Mahāsudarśana was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; he surpassed human complexion and had not yet attained divine complexion. That, Great King, is how King Mahāsudarśana was handsome and beautiful to behold.
He was gracious, having transcended human beauty yet not yet attained divine beauty;
this is called the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of King Mahāsudarśana.

Furthermore, Great King, King Mahāsudarśana was free from illness and of a healthy constitution; he possessed a digestive system that was balanced, neither too hot nor too cold, unafflicted, and pleasant according to the seasons, by which whatever he ate, drank, chewed, or tasted was properly and easily digested. Great King, that King Mahāsudarśana was free from illness and of a healthy constitution, as previously described.
This is called the supernatural power of King Mahāsudarśana.

Furthermore, Great King, King Mahāsudarśana was dear and pleasing to the people of the towns and countryside, just as a father is to his sons. Likewise, Great King, the people of the towns and countryside were dear and pleasing to King Mahāsudarśana, just as sons are to a father. At one time, Great King, the king...

As Mahāsudarśana was departing for the park grounds, he addressed his charioteer: "Charioteer, drive the chariot slowly, very slowly, so that I may behold the merchants and the people of the countryside after a long, long time."
"Matsumura, I shall ask.
The merchants and country folk also addressed the charioteer: "O charioteer, drive the chariot very slowly and gently for a while, so that we may behold the King after a long, long time."
Matsumura [says]: "We shall ask:

Great King, just as King Mahāsudarśana was dear and pleasing to the people of the towns and countryside—just as a father is to his sons—so too were the people of the towns and countryside dear and pleasing to King Mahāsudarśana—just as [sons are] to a father."
"O sons, this is called the supernatural power of King Mahāsudarśana."
MSuAv [6] Then, at another time, the merchants and countryfolk, taking with them abundant gold and bullion, as well as a precious gem and a precious woolen blanket, approached King Mahāsudarśana.
Having approached him, they said this to King Mahāsudarśana: "Sire, we have brought this abundant gold and bullion, a precious gem, and a precious woolen blanket for Your Majesty."

"Therefore, may Your Majesty accept this out of compassion. "Enough, village headman; I already possess such wealth as this," he said, and did not consent. A second and even a third time, the merchants and countryfolk [spoke] to King Mahāsudarśana.

They said this: "We have brought a great quantity of gold and bullion, as well as precious gems and precious woolen blankets, for the sake of the King. May the King accept them out of compassion. For a second and even a third time, King Mahāsudarśana spoke thus to the merchants and countryfolk.

"Enough, village headman! I already possess such a collection of wealth as this," he said, and did not accept [the offer]. Then this thought occurred to the merchants and country folk: "It would not be fitting for us that we have brought so much gold and bullion, as well as precious gems and precious woolen blankets, for the sake of the King."
"If we were to take our respective dwellings once again,
what if we were instead to scatter a great heap of gold and bullion before King Mahāsudarśana, set aside a precious gem and a woolen blanket to one side, and say: 'O Lord, this is your wealth.'"

"Having said this, let us depart without further concern. Thus the merchants and countryfolk, having scattered a great heap of gold and bullion before King Mahāsudarśana and having set aside a precious gem and a woolen blanket to one side, said:
"This is yours."
"O King, this is our accumulated wealth," they said, and having spoken thus, they departed without looking back.
Then, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudarśana: "I have acquired this mass of wealth through righteousness, not through unrighteousness. What if I were to have a righteous palace constructed?
The eighty-four thousand vassal kings heard that King Mahāsudarśana was intent on having a righteous palace constructed. Having heard this, they went to where King Mahāsudarśana was.
They approached him.
Having approached, they said this to King Mahāsudarśana: "May Your Majesty be of little concern regarding the righteous palace; we shall cause a righteous palace to be built for Your Majesty.
"Enough, Matsumura, enough! [he replied].

"Village chiefs, I possess this kind of wealth," he said, and yet he did not accept [the offer]. A second and even a third time, the eighty-four thousand minor kings spoke thus to King Mahāsudarśana: "Be of little concern."
"May the King build a righteous palace! We shall construct a righteous palace for the King. For a second and even a third time, King Mahāsudarśana said this to the eighty-four thousand minor kings:
"Enough, village chiefs! I already possess such a collection of wealth. Having said this, he did not consent.
Then some of those minor kings fell at the feet of King Mahāsudarśana.
Some raised their arms; some grasped the corners of their robes;
and some, having extended their joined palms toward King Mahāsudarśana, said this to King Mahāsudarśana: "May Your Majesty be free from anxiety."
"From the righteous palace. We shall have a righteous palace built for the King. King Mahāsudarśana gave his assent to the eighty-four thousand vassal kings by remaining silent.

Then, the eighty-four thousand vassal kings, understanding the King Mahāsudarśana’s assent through his silence, went to their respective territories and, taking with them abundant gold and bullion, each one—
They approached King Mahāsudarśana where he was at the jeweled pillar;
having approached, they said this to King Mahāsudarśana: "Where, O Lord, shall we construct the righteous palace for Your Majesty?

And how large shall it be? He replied: "Therefore, O village chiefs, construct the righteous palace to the east of Kuśāvatī, one *yojana* in length and one *yojana* in width. "So be it, O Lord," [they replied]. Eighty-four...
Having given their word to King Mahāsudarśana, thousands of provincial kings had a righteous palace constructed to the east of Kuśāvatī, one yojana in length and one yojana in width.
O Great King, in that righteous palace—
Four kinds of staircases had been constructed in the past, made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.
In the Dharmya palace, four kinds of steps were laid out.
They were made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.
In the Dharma palace, four kinds of pillars were erected: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. Of the golden [pillar],...

For the silver pillar, the capital, the triple-ring, the pinnacle, and the *gosāraka* were fashioned of gold; for the lapis lazuli pillar, they were fashioned of crystal; and for the crystal pillar, the capital, the triple-ring, the pinnacle, and the *gosāraka* were fashioned of lapis lazuli. In the Dharmya palace, four kinds of hanging ornaments were fashioned: those made of gold and those made of silver.
They were made of beryl and crystal.
In the Dharmya palace, four kinds of excellent food were prepared: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.
In the Dharmya palace...
The four types of baladharaṇī railings were constructed: made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal.
In the Dharmya palace, four types of turrets were constructed: made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal.
MSuAv [10.8] The righteous palace was covered with four kinds of planks: made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal.
MSuAv [10.9] In the righteous palace, four kinds of staircases were constructed: made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal.
MSuAv [10.10] The righteous palace was surrounded by four kinds of railings:
made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. Of the golden railing, the support, the base, the crossbar, and the marker were fashioned of silver;
of the silver [railing], [the support, base, crossbar, and marker were fashioned of gold].
It was made of gold;
with a base made of beryl, there was a support made of crystal;
with a base made of crystal, there was a support made of beryl; thus the measuring-line was established as a marker.

MSuAv [10.11] In the righteous palace, four kinds of gabled chambers were constructed: those made of gold, those made of silver, those made of beryl, and those made of crystal. In the golden gabled chamber, a silver couch was placed, covered with a cloth of fine silk, a woolen rug, a cotton mattress, a variegated coverlet, a white woolen rug, a *palalikā* rug, and a *kāliṅga* blanket as an underlay; it was provided with a canopy above and red pillows on both sides.

In the silver gabled chamber there was a golden couch; in the lapis lazuli gabled chamber there was a crystal couch; and in the crystal gabled chamber, O Great King, a lapis lazuli couch was set out, spread with a silken cloth.
It was spread with woolen rugs, stuffed mattresses, embroidered coverlets, fine woollen blankets, and deer-skin rugs; it was provided with a canopy above and red pillows on both sides.

In front of the gabled pavilion made of gold, a palm tree made of silver was constructed, complete with leaves, flowers, and fruit made of gold. In front of the one made of silver was one made of gold;
in front of the one made of beryl was one made of crystal.
In front of the gabled pavilion made of crystal, a palmyra tree made of beryl was fashioned, with leaves, flowers, and fruit made of crystal.
When those palmyra trees were stirred by the wind, this kind of charming sound issued forth, just like the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble played perfectly by a skilled musician.

MSuAv [10.14] The righteous palace was strewn with golden sand, sprinkled with sandalwood water, covered with a lattice of gold, and adorned with golden rings. MSuAv [11] Then, eighty-four thousand provincial kings, having learned that the righteous palace had been completed in every respect, constructed in front of the righteous palace a righteous lotus pond, one *yojana* in length and one *yojana* in width.
The Dharmya lotus pond was constructed with four kinds of bricks: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. In this Dharmya lotus pond, there were four kinds of staircases.

They were constructed of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. The Dharma lotus-pools were surrounded by four kinds of railings made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. Great King, on the golden railing, a silver handrail, base, and crossbar were constructed;
on the silver one, a golden one.

The supporting base and the indicator for the crystal [structure] were constructed from beryl, and the supporting base and indicator for the beryl [structure] were constructed from crystal. In the Dharmya lotus pond, various kinds of aquatic flowers were planted, namely:
the utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, saugandhika, and mṛdugandhika; they were seasonal, perennial, and unobstructed for all people. O Great King, in the Dharmya [pond]...

On both banks of the lotus pond, various kinds of land-growing garlands were planted, such as the *atimukta*, *campaka*, *pāṭalā*, *vārṣikā*, *mallikā*, *navamālikā*, *sumanā*, *yūthikā*, and *dhānuṣkārī*. These were seasonal, perennial, and unobstructed for all people. The Dharma-lotus pond was strewn with golden sand, sprinkled with sandalwood water, covered by a network of gold, and adorned with golden bracelets.

MSuAv [12] Then eighty-four thousand minor kings, having learned that the Dharmya Puṣkariṇī had been entirely completed by Jātakṛtaniṣṭhita, caused a Dharmya Tāla grove to be laid out in front of the Dharmya Puṣkariṇī, one yojana in length and one yojana in width. O Great King, in the Dharmya Tāla grove, four kinds of *tāla* trees were planted: those made of gold, those made of silver, those made of beryl, and those made of crystal. Of the golden [tree]...
The leaf, flower, and fruit of the palm tree were fashioned of silver; those of the silver one were of gold;
those of the lapis lazuli one were of crystal;
and those of the crystal one were of lapis lazuli.

It was laid out. When those palm trees were stirred by the wind, this kind of charming sound issued forth, just like that of a five-piece musical ensemble skillfully played by a master musician. The Dharmya palm grove was surrounded by four kinds of railings made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.
[The first railing] was made of gold.
For the railing, a silver support and base was constructed; for the silver [railing], a golden one;
for the beryl [railing], a crystal one;
and for the crystal [railing], a beryl support.

The foundation was laid, and the hall was constructed. A righteous palm grove appeared, strewn with golden sand, sprinkled with sandalwood water, draped with nets of gold, and covered with golden anklets.

Then, the eighty-four thousand vassal kings, having seen the righteous palace, the righteous lotus pond, and the righteous palm grove—all of which were completed according to every tradition—approached King Mahāsudarśana.

They approached him. Having approached King Mahāsudarśana, they said this to him: "Your Majesty, the righteous palace, the righteous lotus pond, and the righteous grove of palm trees have all been completed according to the king's every wish; it is now time for Your Majesty to do as you see fit. Then, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudarśana:
"It would not be fitting for me to enter the righteous palace for the very first time in such a manner."

"I shall dwell in contentment. Suppose I were to invite those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are esteemed as virtuous and dwell within my realm, feed them in the Palace of Dharma, and clothe each of them individually with a pair of new cotton garments. Then King Mahāsudarśana invited those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who were esteemed as virtuous and dwelt within his realm, fed them in the Palace of Dharma, and [clothed each of them individually...]

He covered it with a pair of new fine cloths. Then, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudarśana: "It would not be fitting for me, while staying in my righteous palace, to play, enjoy myself, and amuse myself, fully endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure. What if I were to ascend to the righteous palace?"
"I shall practice the celibate life of a royal seer with only a single attendant.
Then King Mahāsudarśana, having ascended the righteous palace,
practiced the celibate life of a royal seer with only a single attendant.

MSuAv [14] Then King Mahāsudarśana, having entered a gabled chamber made of gold and sat down cross-legged on a couch made of silver, dwelt having attained the first dhyāna— detached from sensual desires, detached from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, characterized by zest and bliss. Having descended from the silver couch and emerged from the golden gabled chamber, he entered a gabled chamber made of silver.

Sitting cross-legged upon a golden couch, he dwells having attained the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires. Then, descending from the golden couch and emerging from the silver gabled chamber, [he approaches] the beryl one.
Having entered the gabled chamber, he sat cross-legged upon a crystal couch; secluded from sensual desires, he dwelt having attained and realized the first dhyāna.
Then, descending from the crystal couch and exiting the gabled chamber made of beryl, he entered a crystal gabled chamber and [sat] upon a beryl couch.
Sitting cross-legged, secluded from sensual desires, he dwelt having attained the first *dhyāna*.
Then, eighty-four thousand women approached the Woman-Jewel (*strīratna*); having approached, they said this to the Woman-Jewel: "O Queen, you should know that we have not seen her for a long time."
"O Lord, we are parched with thirst for the sight of the Lord;

we wish to see the Lord. "In that case, sisters, wait here while I look for the Jewel of the General. Then, having summoned the Jewel of the Woman and the Jewel of the General by means of a messenger, he said this: "O General, you should know this:"
“It has been a long time since we have seen you, O Lord;
I shall assemble eighty-four thousand minor kings,
eighty-four thousand elephants headed by the Naga king Upoṣadha,
and eighty-four thousand horses.

There were eighty-four thousand chariots headed by the horse-king Vālāha, and eighty-four thousand chariots headed by the chariot Nandīghoṣa. Having given their assent, saying "So be it," all those ladies became adorned in yellow ornaments, wearing yellow garments, with yellow garlands, jewelry, and ointments, and surrounded by yellow retinues. Then the Jewel of the Commander-in-Chief [addressed] the eighty-four thousand provincial kings.
Having assembled eighty-four thousand nāgas headed by the nāga king Poṣadha,
and eighty-four thousand horses headed by the horse king Vālāha;
Having assembled eighty-four thousand chariots, headed by the chariot Nandīghoṣa,
and having placed the Jewel of Women upon the chariot Nandīghoṣa,
Having placed the remaining women each upon individual chariots,
they departed from Kuśāvatī and approached the Dharmya Palace. At that time, there arose beneath the Dharmya Palace a loud and great clamor, a roar from a vast multitude of people.

MSuAv [16] King Mahāsudarśana heard from beneath the Palace of Dharma a loud noise, a great clamor, and the roar of a vast multitude of people. Having heard this, he addressed his attendant: (GBM 1561.5)

"O man, what is this loud noise, this great clamor, and the roar of a vast multitude of people beneath the Palace of Dharma? Your Majesty, these eighty-four thousand women, headed by the Woman-Jewel, stand beneath the Palace of Dharma desiring to see the King;
as do eighty-four thousand vassal kings, headed by the Counsellor-Jewel."
Eighty-four thousand elephants headed by the Naga King Upoṣadha;
eighty-four thousand horses headed by the horse-king Vālāha;
and eighty-four thousand chariots.

The chariot Nandīghoṣa and others stood beneath the Dharmya Palace. Then King Mahāsudarśana addressed his attendant: "Well then, my good man, prepare a golden throne beneath the Dharmya Palace, where I may sit and look upon the great multitude of people. "As you command, Your Majesty," replied the attendant to King Mahāsudarśana.

Having given his word, he prepared a golden throne beneath the Palace of Dharma and approached King Mahāsudarśana. Having approached, he said this to King Mahāsudarśana: "A golden throne has been prepared for Your Majesty beneath the Palace of Dharma; may Your Majesty now consider it the right time.
Then King Mahāsudarśana beheld the Palace of Dharma.
Descending from the palace— at the base of the Palace of Dharma—
all those women were adorned in yellow ornaments, wearing yellow garments, with yellow garlands, jewelry, and ointments, and surrounded by yellow retinues. Having seen this, he [thought] as follows:

It occurred to her: "Alas, this woman-folk are truly alluring! Having realized this, she cast her gaze upward. Seeing King Mahāsudarśana casting his gaze upward, the Jewel among Women thought again: "Since the Lord casts his gaze upward upon seeing us, surely the Lord will have no further need for us. Then King Mahāsudarśana...

Having descended from the Dharmya palace and sat upon a golden auspicious throne, the Jewel among Women approached King Mahāsudarśana. Having approached, she prostrated at the feet of King Mahāsudarśana and said this to him: "Your Majesty, here are eighty-four thousand women; may Your Majesty take pleasure in them and let Your Majesty show them favor."
While he was still living, there were eighty-four thousand minor kings headed by the Jewel of the Commander-in-Chief;
eighty-four thousand elephants headed by the Naga King Uposadha; and eighty-four thousand... [GBM 1563.2]
There were thousands of horses, headed by Vālāha, the king of horses;
eighty-four thousand chariots, headed by the chariot Nandīghoṣa;
and eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kuśāvatī. (GBM 1563.3)
"O Goddess, let the Queen generate a sense of affection; let Your Majesty have regard for my life. Formerly, O sister, you treated me with the kindness of a friend, but now you treat me as an enemy.
[18] Then the Woman-Jewel, having been addressed by King Mahāsudarśana with the words "sister," wept and shed tears.
And he spoke thus:

"Since Your Majesty addresses us with the title 'sister,' it will not be long before we shall experience separation, parting, dissociation, and disjunction from Your Majesty. Then the Jewel among Women wiped away her tears with her garment.
“Determination of the School Affiliation of Buddhist Texts Based on Linguistic Criteria,” in *Zur Schulzugehörigkeit von Werken der Hīnayāna-Literatur* (Symposium on Buddhist Studies, III,1),
edited by H. Bechert, Göttingen 1985 (AAWG, 149).
First Part, p.

73, note 46: [puñjya], having prostrated at the feet of King Mahāsudarśana, addressed King Mahāsudarśana as follows: "In what manner, O Lord, do we now treat Your Majesty with friendliness rather than with enmity? Come, sister!"
Speak thus: "O King, the life of humans is brief; the next world must be faced.

One must perform what is wholesome and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). There is no such thing as not dying for one who is born. Furthermore, O King, that moment, instant, or hour in which the total casting off of the body will occur for Your Majesty is not known."

Whatever desire, passion, affection, love, attachment, dependence, or resolve Your Majesty has toward the eighty-four thousand women—may Your Majesty abandon that; may Your Majesty become indifferent even toward life. Whatever [desire Your Majesty has] toward the eighty-four thousand minor kings headed by the Jewel of the General, or toward the eighty-four thousand elephants headed by the Naga King Upoṣadha—(GBM 1564.3)
Among the eighty-four thousand horses headed by the horse-king Vālāha,
among the eighty-four thousand chariots headed by the chariot Nandīghoṣa, and among the eighty-four thousand... [GBM 1564.4]

"In thousands of cities, headed by the royal capital Kuśāvatī, let the King abandon desire, passion, affection, love, attachment, dependence, or obsession; let the King become indifferent toward life. For in this way, sister, you should behave toward the King as a friend, not as an enemy.
[MSuAv 19] "Now, O King, we..."
We conduct ourselves with friendliness, not with hostility. O King, the life of human beings is brief; the hereafter must be faced, and what is wholesome must be done.

The holy life (*brahmacarya*) must be practiced. For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying. O King, even that moment, that instant, that brief duration is not known when the laying down of your body will occur in every respect. O King, let your desire, passion, affection, love, attachment, dependence, or obsession regarding your eighty-four thousand women be abandoned; let the King become indifferent toward life.
He who [was honored] among the eighty-four thousand minor kings of the gods, headed by the Jewel-General;
among the eighty-four thousand nāgas, headed by the Nāga King Upoṣadha; and among the eighty-four thousand... (GBM 1565.2)
Among the thousands of horses headed by the horse-king Vālāha;
among the eighty-four thousand chariots headed by the chariot Nandīghoṣa;
and among the eighty-four thousand cities headed by the royal capital Kuśāvatī.
“May the King abandon desire, passion, affection, love, attachment, dependence, or obsession; may the King become indifferent toward life.

Then King Mahāsudarśana, exhorted by this jewel among women with this instruction, ascended the righteous palace, entered a golden gabled chamber, and sat cross-legged upon a silver couch, accompanied by a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

With a mind free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having resolved upon and suffused one direction, and having attained it.

Likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere and in all respects, he dwells having suffused this entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from enmity, free from rivalry, and free from ill will.

Having resolved upon one direction with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he pervades it, attains it, and dwells therein. Descending from his silver couch, emerging from the golden gabled chamber, entering the silver gabled chamber, and sitting cross-legged on the golden couch, he dwells having attained and pervaded [the state] with a mind accompanied by compassion, free from enmity, and so forth.

Descending from the golden couch, emerging from the silver gabled chamber, entering the beryl gabled chamber, and sitting cross-legged upon the crystal couch, he dwells having pervaded and attained mastery with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy (*muditā*), up to the point of being resolved [upon it]. Descending from the crystal couch, emerging from the beryl gabled chamber, and entering the crystal gabled chamber...
Seated cross-legged upon a couch made of beryl, he dwelt having suffused and attained mastery through a mind accompanied by equanimity, as far as he could resolve.
Then King Mahāsudarśana [addressed] the four Brahmās...

Having cultivated the [four] abodes and abandoned sensual desire for sense-pleasures, by dwelling frequently therein, he was reborn in the fellowship of the Brahma-world. This is the case of King Mahāsudarśana.
The sensation at the time of death was experienced by him, just as a strong man who has eaten a fine meal might experience a momentary fatigue from eating.
Great King, from here to Kuśinagarī— [as far as] GBM 1566.6—
And from the river Hiraṇyavatī as far as the twin śāla grove,
and as far as the Mallas’ Mukuṭabandhana Caitya— in this vicinity spanning twelve yojanas— the Tathāgata stayed for six nights.
This was the seventh time that the body of an anointed Kṣatriya king has been laid down here. And as for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, O Great King,

I do not perceive any spot on earth— whether in the eastern direction, or the southern, or the western, or the northern direction— where the eighth laying down of the body of a Tathāgata has occurred.
It will come to pass. For what reason?
Because, O Great King, the Tathāgata’s way of perceiving existence has been utterly severed.
The cycle of birth has been exhausted; now there is no further existence. // 1 // Thus.
The intermediate summary verse:
the eastern placement, the pillars, the crossbeams, the food-offerings, the strength-sustaining forest, the gate-towers;
the planks, the stairs, the railings, the pinnacles, and the bolts. (2) Thus.
MSuAv [23] Then King Mahāsudarśana, having fed five hundred pratyekabuddhas in the Dharmya Palace and having clothed each one with a pair of fine cotton garments, spoke this verse:
"Having attained such vast wealth, the wise man should not be heedless."
One should give to those endowed with perfected conduct, where offerings reach their fulfillment.
Having given thus in this world with a faithful and liberated mind, the wise and intelligent person shall be reborn in a world of happiness free from affliction. (4) Thus it is said.

"Great King, it might be thought that at that time and on that occasion, the universal monarch named Mahāsudarśana, the lord of the four continents and endowed with the seven jewels and the four human supernormal powers, was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way; it was indeed I who was he at that time."

“At that time, on that occasion, there was a great king named Mahāsudarśana, a wheel-turning monarch, lord of the four continents, endowed with the seven jewels and possessing the four human superpowers.
It might occur to you, Great King, that by means of that gift or that distribution of gifts, I attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way. Rather, that gift is merely a cause, merely a condition, and merely a provision for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The Mahāsudarśanāvadāna is completed.
